To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a 2-km thick, 20-km wide, 10- to 15-Ma-old, south-dipping duplex was formed along the India-Asian suture during the Oligocene-Miocene, and (2) this duplex was exhumed in the late Miocene, and is now exposed at the surface in the Lazi region of southern Tibet.

1) a major phase of deformation and metamorphism in southern Tibet occurred during the late Oligocene–early Miocene; 2) this phase is characterized by widespread development of high-pressure, low-temperature (HP–LT) eclogite-facies assemblages; and 3) this phase of deformation was associated with widespread development of duplexes in the India–Asia suture zone.

(1) the Lazi region is characterized by a series of north-dipping, low-temperature, ductile shear zones; (2) the ductile shear zones are characterized by a consistent, low-temperature deformation history; and (3) the ductile shearing was likely driven by a combination of the southward motion of India and the northward extrusion of the Gangdese batholith.
